Meituan stock faces 10-day Shenzhen drone delivery pause
sum: Meituan's drone-delivery operation in Shenzhen faces a temporary suspension ahead of next week's APEC summit. The company said deliveries in the city were halted for 10 days from Wednesday, November 11, at the request of regulators, with no resumption date announced. Routes in other cities are unaffected, Reuters reported on Friday, November 13.

The report places Meituan among operators running regular drone-delivery routes in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen and at the Great Wall. The network has supported hundreds of thousands of deliveries, bringing food, coffee and drinks to parks, tourist sites and other locations where conventional couriers can have difficulty finding customers.

Shenzhen's pause comes as China promotes a broader low-altitude economy covering airspace up to about 1,000 meters. Civil aviation authorities said 3.29 million drones had been registered by the end of 2025, while annual drone flight hours rose nearly 70 percent to 45.3 million. The figures underline the scale of the infrastructure and regulatory environment surrounding commercial drone use.

The immediate operational effect is geographically limited because Meituan's other drone routes continue to operate. The temporary halt nevertheless highlights the importance of regulatory approvals for a delivery model that depends on access to low-altitude airspace, especially in high-profile cities hosting major international events.

The report did not provide a financial estimate for the Shenzhen suspension. For investors, the relevant near-term questions are whether deliveries restart after the 10-day period and whether regulators impose similar restrictions during other large public events. The broader commercial rollout remains a longer-term test of whether drone delivery can complement Meituan's established food-delivery network.

Meituan stock: CNY 8 billion bond deal extends refinancing horizon
sum: Meituan launched a CNY 8 billion dual-tranche offshore yuan bond on October 27, with the proceeds intended mainly to refinance existing offshore debt and support general corporate purposes. The transaction gives investors a clearer view of the company's financing schedule through 2036.

The The Standard, citing Reuters and a term sheet, reported that the issue comprises CNY 4.5 billion of five-year senior notes and CNY 3.5 billion of 10-year senior notes. The shorter tranche carries a 2.50 percent yield and matures on November 3, 2031. The longer tranche carries a 3.10 percent yield and matures on November 3, 2036.

Combined orders exceeded CNY 20 billion before launch, according to the report. Meituan had previously been targeting about CNY 7 billion, making the final CNY 8 billion transaction larger than that earlier target. The pricing also tightened from initial guidance of about 2.90 percent for the five-year notes and 3.60 percent for the 10-year notes.

The notes are senior unsecured debt rather than equity. The financing therefore does not directly increase Meituan's share count, while the debt being refinanced, the eventual interest burden and the company's ability to manage maturities remain relevant for shareholders. The bonds are expected to receive Baa1 ratings from Moody's and BBB+ ratings from S&P Global Ratings and Fitch, with negative outlooks reported for all three issuer ratings.

sum: Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index closed the week of 2–6 November 2026 at 24,481.86, up 5.10%, its best week since early March, as investors rotated out of AI hardware into discounted Chinese internet platforms and Beijing stepped up market support. China’s inflation and trade data and Singles’ Day headline next week.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, ended Friday 6 November 2026 at 24,481.86, down 315.12 points or 1.27% on the day. For the week, it gained 1,187.44 points, or 5.10%, from the previous Friday’s close of 23,294.42, its largest weekly advance since the first week of March 2026.

The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index rose 5.24% over the week to 8,274.10, and the Hang Seng Tech Index surged about 8.6%. Even so, the benchmark remains well below its 52-week high of about 28,056, leaving room for further recovery.

Hong Kong rose for four straight sessions. The index gained 0.42% to 23,393.32 on Monday 2 November, led by Xiaomi, CATL, Alibaba and Tencent, then added 0.57% to 23,525.97 on Tuesday and 1.67% to 23,919.50 on Wednesday as global markets rallied after the US midterm elections.

Thursday 5 November was the standout. The Hang Seng soared 877.48 points, or 3.67%, to 24,796.98, its best day since February 2025, while the Hang Seng Tech Index jumped 5.55%, its biggest gain of the year. On Friday the global AI sell-off caught up with Hong Kong, and the index fell 1.27%, but it held on to most of the week’s gains.

The rally was a rotation. As investors sold AI hardware stocks in the US, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, they bought Chinese internet platforms that had become cheap: the Hang Seng Tech Index traded at around 13 times forward earnings in October, its lowest valuation since 2024. Thursday’s jump also triggered one of the biggest short squeezes in years.

Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7% on Thursday and Meituan close to 7%. Tencent had already gained almost 6% after launching its new Hunyuan AI model with visual understanding and computer-use capabilities, showing that investors still reward Chinese AI applications even as they sell hardware.

Hong Kong stocks roar back as value rotation boosts Chinese tech
sum: (Nov 5): After languishing for much of the year, Hong Kong stocks are staging a comeback as investors rotate away from hardware stocks into discounted Chinese internet platforms.

The Hang Seng Tech Index climbed 5.6% on Thursday, the most since February 2025. The broader benchmark Hang Seng Index jumped 3.7%, with Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Tencent Holdings Ltd among the biggest drivers behind the advance.

China’s beaten-down internet giants have emerged as a key beneficiary from the US midterm election fallout, as investors pivot away from the artificial intelligence (AI) trade and into value and consumer shares. Alibaba and Tencent offer low valuations with sprawling businesses that touch almost every corner of daily life. Beijing’s renewed efforts to restore investor confidence are also helping the rebound.

Hong Kong stocks are benefitting from several rotation trends in Asia, said Marvin Chen, a strategist at Bloomberg Intelligence. “A North Asia regional rotation into China as Korea and Taiwan come under pressure; a value rotation as China has been stuck at trough valuations this year while the rest of the world rallied; and an AI rotation as investors diversify away from tech hardware and pure AI plays,” he added.

The rebound follows a tough stretch for Hong Kong equities, which remains one of the worst-performing markets globally this year. The Hang Seng Tech Index had come close to erasing all its gains since China’s 2024 stimulus pivot, underscoring the extent of investor scepticism.
Some investors are trying to do “bottom fishing” as Hong Kong names have become very cheap, said Leonid Mironov, a portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital.
Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7%, while food delivery firm Meituan added 6.8%. The Hang Seng Tech gauge traded at 13 times forward earnings estimate last month, the lowest since 2024.

sum: Hong Kong stocks staged their strongest rally in 21 months on Thursday 5 November 2026 as investors rotated out of AI hardware and into discounted Chinese internet platforms, sparking one of the biggest short squeezes in years.

The Hang Seng Index, the benchmark for the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 24,796.98 points on Thursday 5 November 2026, up 877.48 points, or 3.67 percent. The index opened at 24,316.94 and traded between 24,281.77 and 24,871.92, finishing close to the top of its range, a sign that buying pressure persisted throughout the session.

It was the Hang Seng's best day since February 2025, when the index jumped about 4 percent during the DeepSeek-driven technology rally. The benchmark is now up roughly 8 percent from its 22 October low, although it remains well below its 52-week high of about 28,056 and only modestly above its 52-week low near 22,518.

The Hang Seng Tech Index climbed 5.6 percent, its largest gain since February 2025, according to Bloomberg. During the morning session the tech gauge touched about 4,165 points, a gain of nearly 6 percent, and it has now risen for five consecutive sessions, adding roughly 9 percent since the previous Friday.

Even after that surge, the Hang Seng Tech Index remains down about 26 percent for 2026, underlining how severe the earlier sell-off in Chinese internet stocks had been. Bloomberg noted that the index traded at around 13 times forward earnings in October, its cheapest valuation since 2024, which helped attract bargain hunters once the catalyst arrived.

Alibaba Group and Tencent Holdings were among the biggest contributors, each rising more than 7 percent, while Meituan added close to 7 percent at the close after leading heavyweights with a gain of more than 9 percent at midday. NetEase and Xiaomi also climbed by more than 7 percent during the morning session.

Because Alibaba and Tencent are among the largest constituents of both the Hang Seng Index and the Hang Seng Tech Index, their gains account for a large share of the benchmark's 877-point advance. The rally was broad, however, with consumer and internet platforms leading and financials such as the H-share financials index also posting gains of close to 2 percent.

sum: On October 29, 2026: price 69.20 HKD, trend sideways, RSI 38.3, support 69.20, resistance 77.10. technical analysis of meituan stock. Peak — full details here.

Meituan's Hong Kong-listed shares closed at 69.20 HKD on Thursday, October 29, 2026, down 2.81% on the day and sitting just 0.40 HKD above the 3-month low of 68.80, according to exchange data. Over five days the stock has lost 2.95%, and over one month 1.77%. Those monthly figures look mild. The 3-month range tells a harsher story: the high was 96.45.

That gap between a shallow monthly decline and a deep drop from the quarterly peak is the context for today's move. The stock has been sliding for longer than the last 30 days, and it is now testing the floor of its recent range.

Technically, the trend is classed as sideways. The 20-day moving average, which smooths the last 20 trading days of prices into one line, edged down just 0.08% over five days. A flat average suggests the stock has not been in a sharp, accelerating slide recently, but it also shows no sign of recovery.

The price is below the 20-day average of 72.34, which in turn sits under the 50-day average of 75.13. This stacking, with price under the short average and the short average under the long one, is a classic bearish arrangement. It means recent buyers are, on average, holding losses. No new moving-average crossover has formed.

As shown in the chart, the price has settled right on the 20-day support at 69.20, the very level where it closed. Resistance over the same window stands at 77.10. With the price at 0% of that range, the stock sits at the very bottom of its recent trading band.

Momentum gauges paint a mixed picture. The 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI), which measures the speed of recent gains against losses on a 0-100 scale, reads 38.3. That is neutral, though leaning weak; readings below 30 are usually called oversold.

items.t: Kimi K3 Wipes $3.3T From Chip Stocks: Moonshot Moves Toward Hong Kong IPO
sum: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released July 16 at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, erased more than $3.3 trillion in global semiconductor market value in a matter of days — and on Sunday, the Beijing-based startup responded to its own market-moving moment by circulating a shareholder resolution seeking approval for a Hong Kong initial public offering within six months.

The selloff drove the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index more than 20% below its late-June peak, crossing the technical threshold for a bear market. It marked the worst weekly rout for chipmakers since April 2025. Before any enterprise buyer routes sensitive code or business logic through the Kimi API, one number deserves to sit next to the cost comparison: independent testing found K3's hallucination rate climbed to approximately 51% even as its raw accuracy improved — meaning roughly one in two factual assertions from the model may be wrong. The full model weights needed for independent verification are not scheduled for public release until July 27.

Kimi K3 is a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model — the largest open-weight AI system ever released — with a 1-million-token context window and native vision support. The 2.8-trillion figure is the total parameter count across all 896 specialized expert subnetworks, but only 16 of those experts activate for any given token, meaning the model's per-token compute cost is closer to 30–50 billion active parameters in practice. That sparse-routing architecture is what makes a model of this size economically viable to serve.
Three architectural innovations distinguish K3 from its predecessor, Kimi K2.6:

Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) replaces standard quadratic self-attention in most layers with a more efficient hybrid linear attention, interleaving full attention with linear attention in a 3:1 ratio. In Moonshot's smaller research model, KDA cut key-value cache usage by up to 75% and decoded up to six times faster than a comparison system at 1-million-token context. K3-specific numbers await the July 27 technical report.
Attention Residuals (AttnRes) let each transformer layer selectively retrieve representations from arbitrary earlier layers rather than accumulating them uniformly.

items.t: Alibaba bids $1.5 billion for China grocer Pupu in Meituan fight
sum: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. is offering $1.5 billion to buy Chinese grocery delivery firm Pupu, initiating a bidding war as part of a broader campaign to wrest market share from online commerce rival Meituan.

China’s largest consumer internet platform’s proposed price is more than double an earlier bid from Sun Art Retail, according to people familiar with the matter. Sun Art, a former Alibaba affiliate that’s now backed by private equity firm DCP Capital, had proposed a takeover at $600 million, the people said, asking not to be identified because the sale process is confidential.
Alibaba’s proposal emerged just months after Meituan announced a $717 million acquisition of Dingdong Fresh Holding Ltd., after beating out rival bidders.

Alibaba’s offer underscores its determination to prevail in an intensifying battle between three giants of Chinese online commerce. The rising valuations reflect fierce competition for scarce retail assets, as Alibaba, Meituan and JD.com Inc. step up efforts to dominate local commerce and fresh produce, among the few remaining consumer segments that remain under-penetrated online.

Fujian-based Pupu is among the last independent online grocery companies in China yet to be acquired. China’s grocery platforms have engaged in years of subsidy-driven price wars, pressuring margins and perpetuating “involution” — the destructive competition Beijing is now seeking to reduce.

While consolidation may help curb price wars, it also risks concentrating market power in the hands of a few dominant platforms, potentially conflicting with Beijing’s goal of fostering more competition. Meituan’s proposed acquisition of Dingdong is awaiting approval from antitrust regulators. A Pupu sale to an industry leader may also draw Beijing’s attention.

items.t: 5 Of The Most Popular Apps In China
sum: In China, the most popular apps aren't the giants you'd expect from Google and Meta, and, in fact, there's a good change you've probably never heard of any of them. The FBI warns Android and iPhone users to avoid certain apps that could give the Chinese government access to user data, but using the "Great Firewall of China," it also engages in internet censorship, which includes smartphone apps. This has resulted in ubiquitous Western apps such as Instagram, DoorDash, and YouTube being replaced by Chinese apps Rednote, Bilibili, and Meituan, respectively, as the most popular options among users.

Besides that, China has a unique structure of apps where some of them are known as "super apps," which is the case of Wechat and Alipay. In these platforms, you not only communicate with your family and friends, but you can use it to pay for goodies, watch videos, get train tickets, and more. We've already put together a list of the 14 best apps you should download, but here's everything you need to know about some of the most popular apps in China and how they compare to the options available in the West.

Rednote, which is also known as Xiaohongshu, evolved from a niche travel PDF into a global lifestyle app. It was founded in 2013, and, at the time, was used as a guide for Chinese shoppers traveling abroad. Quickly, it changed its business to blend community reviews with a seamless marketplace. With around 350 million monthly active users, its features focus on multi-image and video posts that have long-form captions making it a visual search engine, similar to Instagram.

The app works as a "utility-driven" platform as it has found success for users trying to get their latest skincare routines, travel itineraries, or other fashion trends before making a purchase. The app itself calls its users as "villagers," as it sees the world as a "global village," where people can connect and communicate. When compared to Instagram, it's possible to see that Rednote is far ahead with its social shopping features, while Meta's app is still exploring these capabilities. After all, Instagram is all about scrolling and seeing what friends and celebrities are doing.

sum: Embodied intelligence startup Galaxea AI has raised 1 billion yuan ($144 million) in a Series B funding round, boosting its valuation to 10 billion yuan.

The financing, announced Wednesday, brought in new investors including Jinding Capital, BAIC Group Industrial Investment Co. Ltd. and Hone Capital. Existing backers such as Cathay Capital, Meituan Dragonball and Capital Today also increased their stakes. The latest deal lifts Galaxea’s total funding to nearly 3 billion yuan.

items.t: Trip.com shares plunge almost 20% as China opens antitrust probe into Asia's largest online travel firm
sum: Shares of Chinese online travel services provider Trip.com plunged 19.23% in Hong Kong on Thursday after Beijing opened an antitrust probe into the company, making it the worst performer in the Hang Seng index.
The fall also marks the stock's worst day in Hong Kong since it was listed in April 2021. Shares had closed 17% lower on Wednesday in New York.

China's State Administration for Market Regulation late Wednesday said it was investigating Trip.com due to "suspected abuse of its dominant market position and monopolistic practices," according to a CNBC translation of the statement in Mandarin.

Trip.com is the largest online travel provider in Asia by market cap, and one of the biggest globally. The company has stakes in UK flight aggregator Skyscanner, Indian travel company MakeMyTrip, as well as several Chinese travel providers.
Trip.com said in a statement it would "actively cooperate" with the investigation, and added its business operations were functioning as usual.
The case could have long term ramifications for the company, according to Morningstar senior equity analyst Kai Wang.

Wang said that "multiple local tourism associations have complained that Trip.com is committing the same violations as the other two platforms, where it is forcing local merchants to sign exclusive agreements with the platform." Trip.com will then increase commissions from the merchants after these agreements are signed.

Hong Kong stocks rise on tech, health as mainland China turnover hits record
sum: Hong Kong stocks rallied on Monday, lifted by gains in healthcare and technology shares, while daily turnover on mainland China’s exchanges surged to a record high.

The Hang Seng Index climbed 1.4 per cent to close at 26,608.48, while the Hang Seng Tech Index climbed 2.9 per cent. On the mainland, the CSI 300 Index advanced 0.65 per cent and the Shanghai Composite Index gained 1.1 per cent.

Trading volume on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges shares hit a record 3.58 trillion yuan (US$513.2 billion), surpassing the previous high of 3.43 trillion yuan on October 8 last year, when stocks surged after China signalled a shift in policies to stabilise growth. Monday’s rally was driven by surging AI-related stocks.

No Free Lunch: China’s Takeout War Wraps Up Without a Winner
sum: For much of this year, China’s three food delivery giants waged an aggressive subsidy war, pouring billions into deep discounts and seasonal promotions to seize market share and lure delivery riders.

But last week, all three companies — Meituan, Ele.me (now Taobao Flash), and JD.com — disclosed steep third-quarter losses, confirming that months of heavy subsidies have taken a steep financial toll.

While Meituan swung to a 16-billion-yuan ($2.3 billion) loss — its biggest since listing — and Alibaba, the parent company of Ele.me, saw its earnings fall by half, JD.com’s new business arm, including its food delivery service, more than doubled its revenue but still lost nearly 16 billion yuan, the companies’ quarterly reports show.

Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper estimated that Meituan, Alibaba, and JD.com together spent nearly 80 billion yuan in subsidies and marketing this year as they fought for dominance in food delivery and instant retail.
Competition between the three platforms intensified after e-commerce giant JD.com began recruiting restaurants and delivery riders in February and formally entered the food delivery market in April.
Throughout the summer, platforms rolled out waves of coupons and promotions — featuring 0 to 1 yuan coffees and milk teas — boosting order volumes but not revenue.
According to a recent report by JPMorgan, Meituan now handles around 71 million daily orders — roughly 50% of the take-out market in China — followed by Alibaba at 42% and JD.com at 8%.

An interval-valued Pythagorean fuzzy TOPSIS approach for service quality evaluation of bike-sharing providers under uncertain environment
sum: Facing the increasing bicycle providers in the market, it becomes a focus problem for companies to improve differentiated service strategies in this fierce market. Prior research has successively carried out service quality evaluation of bike-sharing providers using various quantitative methods. However, lots of methods cannot accurately adjust the representation range of uncertain information. Besides, service quality is involved of various quantifiable and non-quantifiable criteria. Moreover, considering the fact that different people hold different perceptions, it may be difficult for them to make accurate judgments under fuzzy environment. To address the aforementioned issues, this study places a specific research regarding the bike-sharing enterprise service level from four main dimensions, including perceptibility, availability, dependability and sustainability, and a novel group decision making approach is developed to evaluate bike-sharing service quality using extended Techniques for Order Preferences by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) under interval-valued Pythagorean fuzzy environment. The extended group decision making approach is characterized by the interval-valued Pythagorean fuzzy set (IVPFS), which has a good ability to deal with uncertainty, ambiguity and imprecision in the decision-making process, and enables decision makers to make more accurate and reliable judgments with considering the subjective nature of human judgments under fuzzy conditions. Finally, experiments are carried out to verify the viability and effectiveness of the proposed approach, and the results show that the proposed approach is effective and efficient to help decision makers to select optimal bicycle providers.

In recent years, with emerging traffic congestion and air pollution, shared bicycles have become a typical representative of achieving the increasing development of the sharing economy throughout the world. The wide use of shared bicycles in cities can not only reduce traffic congestion, but also effectively solve the problems of air pollution and traffic jam1,2. Bike-sharing at an average growing speed of 37% annually since 2009 has been becoming an increasingly significant component of planning and development of sustainable economy3.
